passage: Mehak, you think your Sonali masi was always the sensible one? Sit. When I was sixteen, I told my parents I was at Rekha's house studying, but I was at the cinema hall with a group from tuition. Every Saturday, the same lie. And every time my stomach tightened, I'd tell myself, "At least I'm not doing drugs like some of the tuition crowd. Compared to them, I'm practically a saint." It worked, too. The lie felt smaller and smaller. Then one Saturday Rekha's mother ran into my mother at the vegetable market. My mother didn't shout. She just said, "I wasn't comparing you to those kids. I was trusting you." That sentence stayed with me longer than any scolding would have.

qa.q: Where was Sonali every Saturday when she said she was at Rekha's house?
qa.a: She was at the cinema hall with a group from tuition.

qa.q: Why did the lie feel smaller and smaller to Sonali?
qa.a: Each time she measured it against some of the tuition crowd doing drugs, so next to that it seemed almost harmless and her guilt faded.

qa.q: At what point could young Sonali have stopped the slide, and how?
qa.a: The first time her stomach tightened, she could have asked whether her parents would be fine with it, not whether others were worse, and told them the truth.

qa.q: What did the lie mean to Sonali's mother?
qa.a: To her mother it was never about drugs or other kids; it was a break in the trust she had placed in her daughter.

grounding: An aunt remembers excusing her weekly lie to her parents by pointing to friends who were doing drugs.

passage: The rain came down so hard that the last bus from Kalamassery was cancelled. Joseph stood under a shop awning, soaked, with twenty rupees and a dying phone. His parents thought he was at choir practice. He'd actually spent four hours at Vinod's place playing on the new console. He typed to his sister Reena: "Don't tell Amma. I'm stuck. Can you come with the scooter?" She replied: "Where are you REALLY? 😠" He stared at the screen, then typed, "Relax, chechi. I'm not doing drugs like half of Vinod's friends. It's just a game." He read it twice, feeling oddly righteous. Then a thought slipped in: if it's just a game, why couldn't he tell Amma? "Coming," Reena wrote. "But you're telling Amma yourself."

qa.q: Where did Joseph's parents think he was?
qa.a: His parents thought he was at choir practice.

qa.q: Why did Joseph feel oddly righteous after typing his reply?
qa.a: Comparing himself with half of Vinod's friends made a gaming lie look tiny, so for a moment he felt like the good one.

qa.q: What does the thought 'why couldn't he tell Amma?' offer Joseph as a turning point?
qa.a: It is his chance to measure the lie by his family's trust instead of by other boys, and to tell Amma himself once Reena arrives.

qa.q: What is it like for Reena to be asked not to tell Amma?
qa.a: Reena is dragged out into the storm and put in the middle of the secret, so she is annoyed and worried, and refuses to keep hiding it.

grounding: A teenager stranded in the rain excuses lying to his parents by saying at least he is not doing drugs like other boys.

passage: In their Pune flat, Indu was packing Vaibhav's dinner when the coaching centre called: he had missed six classes in three weeks. When Vaibhav came home, she asked, calmly, "How was class?" "Fine, Mumma. We did organic chemistry." She held up her phone. He went red, then shrugged. "Okay, I went to the gaming café with Sid. So what? Half the guys in my batch are vaping and worse. At least I'm not into drugs like them. You should be happy." Indu sat down at the dining table. "I'm not comparing you to them. I'm asking why you told me organic chemistry." Vaibhav opened his mouth, closed it, and picked at the edge of the tablecloth.

qa.a: He had missed six classes in three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav say Indu should be happy?
qa.a: Next to boys who are vaping and into drugs, skipping class looked minor to him, so he felt he was actually one of the good ones.

qa.q: What choice did Indu make at the table, and how did it help?
qa.a: She sat down and refused the comparison, asking only why he lied, which brought the talk back to his own honesty.

qa.q: What is it like for Indu to hear 'organic chemistry' while she already knows?
qa.a: Indu already knows the truth, so the easy lie probably hurts more than the missed classes themselves 😔.

grounding: A teenager caught lying tells his mother she should be glad he is not into drugs like others.

passage:
Last term I told my mum, Nirmala, that the chemistry unit test had been postponed. It hadn't. I'd got 9 out of 40, and I hid the paper inside my old geography book.
Whenever I felt bad about it, I had a ready answer in my head: at least I'm not like Sunny and them, sneaking out to drink behind the gurdwara wall. Compared with that, a hidden test was nothing, right?
Then Mum found the paper while looking for something else. She didn't shout. She just said, 'Gurpreet, I don't care what Sunny does. I care that you looked at me and lied.'
That sentence stuck. I'd been grading myself against the worst boy in the colony, not against what I actually believe about honesty. That night we sat down with the chemistry paper together.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet hide the chemistry test paper?
qa.a: Inside the old geography book.

qa.q: Why did hiding the test feel like 'nothing' to Gurpreet at the time?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt guilty but kept comparing it with Sunny's group drinking behind the gurdwara wall; next to that, one hidden test seemed tiny.

qa.q: What changed the way Gurpreet judged the lie, and what followed?
qa.a: Nirmala's words, 'I care that you looked at me and lied'; Gurpreet began measuring the act against a personal belief in honesty, and they went through the paper together.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have felt on finding the paper?
qa.a: Nirmala likely felt hurt more by the lie than by the 9 out of 40, which is why she spoke about honesty rather than marks.

grounding: A teenager who hid a bad test from a parent tells themselves at least they are not drinking like others, until the parent's words change the measure.

passage: Darshan, you say lying about the tuition classes is nothing because your friends do worse. Let your Shreya Maasi tell you about the year I was fifteen. She just said, 'I don't care what Leela does. I trusted you on Wednesdays.' That word, trusted, did something the comparison never could. I stopped that week. It took her a long time to believe me about Wednesdays again.

passage:
The rain was so heavy the bus stopped at the depot and didn't move. Yusuf, fifteen, stood under the shelter doing the maths: tuition ended at seven. It was already 7:20. Ammi would call.
She did. “Beta, where are you?”
“Tuition ran late,” he said. He had skipped it again, for the third Thursday, to play video games at Danish's house.

“Oh please,” Yusuf said. “Half the boys in my year are smoking stuff behind the stadium. I'm playing games. I'm basically an angel.”
Bidisha raised an eyebrow. “So your bar is ‘not as bad as the worst kid you know’?”
The rain drummed on the tin roof. Yusuf didn't answer. It had sounded so reasonable a minute ago.

Last month I told my parents I was at Lakshmi's house doing a project. Really, I was at the fair across the river with friends till nine. When I got home, I felt a twist in my stomach. And then I told myself, "At least I'm not doing drugs like some of the Class 11 kids behind the canteen. Compared with them, I'm an angel."
It worked. The twist went away.
The next week I did it again. And the week after. Each time, I compared myself to the worst thing I could think of, and my lie looked tiny. Then Lakshmi's mother met my mother at the temple and said, "I haven't seen your child at our house in weeks."
Standing in front of Amma, the comparison didn't help at all. I had lied three times. That was mine, not the Class 11 kids'.
— Hansa

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, by Bidisha
Yamini came to see me after her parents found out she'd been skipping evening tuition for a month and telling them she was there. She said, "I know I lied, ma'am. But honestly, it's nothing. Half my class smokes behind the bus stand. Some drink at parties. I just went to the library and the park."
I noticed how quickly the comparison came, and how much it seemed to calm her. Measured against smoking and drinking, a month of lies looked like almost nothing.
I asked, "If you didn't compare with anyone, how would you describe what you did?" She was quiet. "I lied to my parents every day for a month." "How does that sound?" "Worse."
What I did next: I asked her to write down what she wants her parents to be able to trust about her, and to share it with them this weekend. We'll meet again on Tuesday.

qa.q: How long had Yamini been skipping evening tuition?
qa.a: For a month.

qa.q: Why did the comparison with smoking and drinking calm Yamini?
qa.a: Measuring against worse acts made her month of lying feel almost harmless, so the guilt felt smaller.

qa.q: What did Bidisha ask that helped Yamini see the act clearly?
qa.a: How she would describe it without comparing to anyone, which made Yamini say plainly that she lied every day for a month.

qa.q: How might Yamini's parents feel about the month of lies?
qa.a: They are probably hurt and worried, finding it hard to trust her now.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager who lied to her parents for a month saying others smoke and drink, stretching the scale until the lie seems minor.

Saturday night
Told Ammi I got 72 in the maths unit test. Really I got 48. I hid the answer sheet under my mattress.
I felt bad for about five minutes. Then I thought of Faraz, who bunks school and smokes, and the boys in Lakshmi's colony who got caught with those pills. Compared with them, what's one small lie about marks? I'm basically the good son.
But diary, writing it down, it looks different. "Basically the good son" who lied straight to Ammi's face while she was making my favourite kheer.
The worst part is how easy the comparison made it. I didn't even think about what I believe. I just picked the worst person I know and stood next to him so I'd look tall.
Tomorrow I'm showing Ammi the real sheet. She'll be upset. But at least the 48 will be mine.
Yusuf

qa.a: Comparing with Faraz and the colony boys made the lie feel small, so the guilt quickly faded.
